name: OpenCilk (opencilk-project)
baseline: Intel oneTBB, OpenMP and the Cilk Plus runtime (the abstract says only 'the other runtimes'; these three are the back ends the paper added, so they are inferred as the baselines)
workload: 15 benchmark Cilk programs run on the OpenCilk work-stealing runtime (cheetah) versus the other task-parallel runtimes the paper extended OpenCilk to target, geometric mean over the 15 programs at 1 core and at 48 cores.
claimed_speedup: Geometric mean 4%-26% faster than the other runtimes on 1 core and 10%-120% faster on 48 cores across 15 benchmark Cilk programs (PPoPP 2023 abstract, seen as a search-result snippet only; per-runtime split and per-benchmark rows not seen).
hardware: 48-core machine per the abstract; CPU model not seen
stars_or_usage: 132 stars, 39 forks; compiler of the OpenCilk platform (MIT)
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in library: needs the OpenCilk compiler (an LLVM/Clang fork implementing Tapir) and the Cilk language extensions (cilk_spawn, cilk_sync, cilk_for) in C/C++ source. The runtime is a separate repository (OpenCilk/cheetah). The monorepo is a full LLVM tree (546k commits), so building from source is heavy; prebuilt releases exist. Ships Cilksan (race detector) and Cilkscale (scalability analyzer) as companion tools.
caveats: Numbers come from the abstract snippet of 'OpenCilk: A Modular and Extensible Software Infrastructure for Fast Task-Parallel Code' (Schardl and Lee, PPoPP '23, pp. 189-203); the paper itself (ACM, MIT DSpace, SciSpace, PPoPP site, NSF PAR) was unreachable in this environment (host not resolvable), so tables, CPU model, compiler flags, the exact list of 'other runtimes' and the per-runtime geomeans are unseen. Tier B rests on peer review only; no artifact repository was found (the OpenCilk org lists smallapps and applications for regression tests and examples, nothing labelled as the paper's artifact), so A is not supported. The 4%-26% and 10%-120% ranges span several baselines, so the margin against oneTBB or OpenMP alone is unknown and may be the small end. The authors own the compiler, so this is first-party-authored though peer reviewed. Cilk Plus is deprecated and gone from current GCC and ICC, so that baseline is historical. The repo README makes no numeric or named comparison (only 'optimize task-parallel programs more effectively than mainstream compilers'). Weak independent hint, snippet only: Los and Petushkov (arXiv 2410.01222, i7-8700, fine-grained SMT kernels) report their Relic framework 30.1% faster than oneTBB and 21.4% faster than OpenCilk, which implies OpenCilk ahead of oneTBB there (derived, not checked). The repo is a fork of llvm/llvm-project that adds Tapir and Cilk support; licence is the LLVM Apache-2.0 with LLVM exception, and OpenCilk's own changes are MIT with an addendum allowing distribution under the LLVM licence instead. Retier once the paper PDF is readable.

name: Lace (trolando)
baseline: Intel TBB, Cilk Plus (Cilk++), OpenMP and Wool (Wool is the parity target, not a claimed loss)
workload: Fine-grained fork-join benchmarks (fib, UTS, N-Queens, matmul, strassen, cilksort and others from the Cilk-5 suite) timed on multi-core machines; the exact paper table was not seen.
claimed_speedup: No numbers seen. Paper abstract (search snippet): the split deque and the private-deque variant implemented in Lace have 'similar low overhead and high scalability as Wool', i.e. parity with Wool, not faster. Third-party 2020 University of Twente thesis (search snippet): on Unbalanced Tree Search, Fibonacci and Strassen, Lace performs best, CilkPlus and TBB intermediate, OpenMP worst by far; no figures seen.
compiler_and_flags: Repo benchmarks (benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt): C11/C++11, Release builds add -flto, optional -march=native via LACE_NATIVE_OPT; the paper's flags were not seen
stars_or_usage: 61 stars; README cites the author's Sylvan multi-core decision diagram thesis as a user
tradeoffs: C API for fork-join only: tasks are declared with TASK macros and use SPAWN/SYNC/CALL, so it is not a general thread pool with futures. Fixed-size deque and stack set at lace_start. Per-task slot is fixed size (lace32 and lace128 variants trade task size). Workers sleep with exponential backoff when idle, optional hwloc pinning, optional per-worker statistics. Builds on Linux, macOS, Windows (MSVC, MinGW) and FreeBSD.
caveats: No performance numbers on any page opened: the README has none (only 'low-overhead, lock-free work-stealing' and a pointer to docs on the blocked GitHub Pages site), docs/benchmarks.rst lists the benchmark programs and how to run them but has no results, and the repo benchmark CMake builds only Lace and sequential variants, not TBB, Cilk or OpenMP versions, so the repo alone cannot reproduce a comparison. Euro-Par 2014 / MuCoCoS paper 'Lace: Non-blocking Split Deque for Work-Stealing' (van Dijk and van de Pol, LNCS 8806 pp. 206-217, DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-14313-2_18), van Dijk's PhD thesis and the Twente essay (essay.utwente.nl/essays/82071, 'Load balancing framework comparison') were all unreachable here, so the tables with core counts, CPU and flags are unseen; the abstract claims parity with Wool, so against Wool this is not a speed win. The Twente ranking is a bachelor-level thesis seen only as a snippet. Tier C because peer-reviewed and independent evidence exists but no figures were read; retier to B or A once the paper tables or the thesis are read. Lead: docs say the benchmark implementations are adapted from Nowa (Schmaus et al., IPDPS 2021), whose paper may carry a Lace comparison; not checked. The 2.x releases (2.4.0 on 2026-06-07) rewrote parts of the library, so 2014 numbers may not describe the current code.

name: FastThreadPool (komrad36)
baseline: std::async, boost::asio::thread_pool and BS::thread_pool (none measured; no benchmark exists)
workload: None: the repository contains no benchmark code and reports no measurement.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: 'A super fast lock-free (though not always wait-free) thread pool.'
tradeoffs: fast_thread_pool.h (183 lines, header-only) is a lock-free multi-producer multi-consumer linked-list queue of plain function pointers (void (*)()), not a full pool: no worker threads are created by the class, no arguments or return values (no std::function, no futures), one heap allocation per AddWork. Waiters spin with _mm_pause; the README itself says it should sleep instead of spin after a while (TODO) and could be faster with block queues, so idle consumers burn CPU.
caveats: Pure assertion with no numbers and no baseline run; kept as a tier D record because the author (komrad36) is a known performance-oriented developer. The repo has 5 commits, all on 2021-10-18 and 2021-10-19, no tests and no benchmark. The source file carries detailed memory-order annotations (S1-S8, L1-L5) but no correctness proof or test was seen. Not comparable to std::async or BS::thread_pool in features, so any speed claim would need a like-for-like queue benchmark.
